Among them, the inkstone is like the bricks that form this grand structure. At the opening ceremony of the Beijing Olympic Games, the long scroll depicting the 5,000-year-old civilization and history of the Chinese nation unfolded from the Four Treasures of the Study?brush, ink, paper, and inkstone. They are symbols of China's ancient culture and well-deserved national treasures. As one of the Four Treasures of the Study, the inkstone has made outstanding contributions to the dissemination of Chinese history and culture. Among the famous inkstones produced in China, the Duan Inkstone is particularly renowned and ranks first among the "Four Great Famous Inkstones of China". In 2004, Zhaoqing was awarded the title of "Capital of Chinese Inkstones". In 2006, the "Duan Inkstone Craftsmanship" was included in the first batch of China's National Intangible Cultural Heritage List. The ore for Duan Inkstones took approximately 400 million years to form through geological evolution. Among all sources of Duan Inkstone materials, the stones from four key pits?Laokeng (Old Pit), Mazikeng (Sesame Pit), Kengzaiyan (Kengzai Rock), and Songkeng (Song Pit)?are regarded as the finest, collectively known as the "Four Famous Pits" of Duan Inkstones. The production of Duan Inkstones boasts a long history. As early as over 1,300 years ago, during the Tang Dynasty, mining of stone for Duan Inkstones had already begun at Laokeng, marking the official start of its systematic production. In recent years, many of these famous pits have been "closed down". This measure is primarily due to the fact that the raw materials for Duan Inkstones, being non-renewable geological resources, have become increasingly rare and hard to obtain. The closure aims to protect these precious geological heritages and ensure the sustainable inheritance of Duan Inkstone craftsmanship. The crafting process of Duan Inkstones is extremely intricate, consisting of key procedures including stone quarrying, material selection, rough shaping (zhipu), design, carving, box matching, polishing, and waxing. Due to the fact that most raw Duan Inkstone materials are not resistant to vibration, all stages of Duan Inkstone production have long relied entirely on manual work. 147638198604.title: 1944 Omega R17.8 Cal 300 17J Rectangular Movement Dial Hands Runs Strong
147638198604.desc: Offered here is an unusually attractive mid-1940s Omega rectangular wristwatch movement and dial assembly, dating to approximately 1944–1945 and built around Omega's 17-jewel R17.8 movement, later designated caliber 300. This is considerably more interesting than a loose anonymous Omega movement. The assembly retains its beautifully aged Omega-signed shaped dial, original-style gold-tone hands, subsidiary seconds, applied Arabic numerals and markers, winding stem and crown, together with the complete signed 17-jewel movement. Most importantly, the movement runs strongly . A video of the actual movement operating accompanies the photographs. The watch case itself is no longer present, so this is being offered as an excellent restoration candidate, donor assembly or collectible vintage Omega movement/dial set. Dating the Movement The serial number visible on the movement is: 10,457,763 Published Omega production tables place the 10,000,000 serial range beginning around 1944 , while approximately 10.6 million corresponds to 1946. That places movement number 10,457,763 most reasonably around 1944–1945 . Pocket Watch Repair The date is also completely consistent with the movement architecture and dial design. This is therefore a genuine World War II-era / immediate wartime-period Omega movement rather than a later rectangular watch designed to imitate the Art Deco style. Omega R17.8 Movement The movement architecture identifies it with Omega's important R17.8 family . The movement itself is clearly signed: OMEGA WATCH CO. SWISS and: SEVENTEEN 17 JEWELS The movement serial: 10,457,763 is engraved directly into the bridge. The upper bridge is also marked: UNADJUSTED That marking should not be confused with a statement about the quality of the movement. Swiss manufacturers frequently marked movements "unadjusted" for watches destined for certain export markets because import duties historically varied according to jewel count and adjustment specifications. R17.8 and Caliber 300 Omega introduced the R17.8 family around 1940 specifically for shaped rectangular watches. The movement measures approximately 17.8 x 22 mm , allowing Omega to build genuinely rectangular watches rather than placing a round movement inside a rectangular case. Omega's historical caliber records identify the 17-jewel R17.8 version as appearing in 1944 and subsequently designate it caliber 300 under Omega's later numerical caliber system. 128137027372.title: Sixth Plate Daguerreotype, Frontiersman with Rifle and Dog
128137027372.desc: Powerful and arresting sixth plate daguerreotype of a young Hispanic man seated with a percussion rifle upright in his right hand and his left hand resting on the head of a white dog sprawled across his lap. His intense gaze, thick mustache, and dark hair frame a face of striking presence, emphasized by the wide-brimmed black hat, cravat, and satin-trimmed waistcoat he wears. The dog's relaxed posture offers a poignant contrast to the man's upright and armed stance. The composition is similar to Civil War era images of soldiers with rifles posing with their dogs before heading off to war. The sitter's distinctive features and dress suggest possible origins in the American Southwest or Northern Mexico, placing this image in the rare category of early Mexican American or Tejano daguerreotypes with frontier context. The backdrop is plain and studio-bound, directing full attention to the subject's physicality, expression, and symbolism— emblematic of independence, vigilance, and masculine pride. Images of Hispanic sitters from the daguerreian era, particularly armed and accompanied by animals, are of exceptional scarcity. This example is further elevated by its sharp detail, confident pose, and ethnographic resonance - museum-worthy representation of 19th-century frontier identity and personal portraiture. Case front and back do not match each other, but both are included as found. Case has modest wear. (please ignore glare in photos)
